title: THE METALS MEETING
about: The Governor talks his Board of Regents out of democracy and into Metals Week: the Bronze worker's question, the Socratic interrogation of the board, and the quiet chant that becomes law.

beats.text: Night over Austin. In a glass tower above the city, the Governor's Board of Regents sits around a marble table, and a machine counts the mood of the room.
We're losing the narrative.
We're not losing it. We're… experiencing "unexpected interpretation."
A clip is spreading across the state: a Bronze-class worker at the city wall, shouting into a security camera.
see: a worker shouting at a camera

beats.text: If the Noble Lie isn't secret, then why is it called a lie?
And what are they asking for?
Representation.
Say it plainly.
Voting. Seats. Input. "Democracy."

beats.ask: we want a say in who runs things

beats.text: Democracy is not rule by the people. It's rule by the loudest hunger. A democracy of appetites.
His answer is an old story from Plato, the Myth of the Metals. Bronze builds, Silver defends, Gold thinks. Each citizen born to a place.
The Myth of the Metals does one thing better than any constitution ever has: It makes inequality feel… natural.
So the "only thing keeping the state from descending" is… branding?
It's not branding. It's a boundary. Between those who can delay gratification— and those who would vote to eat the future.
Then the Governor questions his own board, the way the old philosopher questioned Athens.
see: men in suits around a table

beats.text: Let's do this Socratically. Answer me: If the Bronze had full power tomorrow, what would they vote for first?
They'd… take.
Take what?
Gold privileges.
And second?
They'd dismantle the Auxiliaries.
Exactly. They would vote until the state becomes a mirror of their wants. That's not freedom. That's a buffet with guns.

beats.ask: if you give people everything they will just want more

beats.text: Out in the Shadow Zone, poets are drawing crowds. His remedy is a festival: Metals Week. Everyone re-graded, a loyalty broadcast, and a brisket voucher for the Bronze.
see: a crowd listening to a man reading aloud
a parade down a main street

beats.text: A merch drop.
A ritual.
Governor… what if you're wrong?
Then history will call me a tyrant. But if I'm right, history won't call me anything at all. Because history requires disorder to be remembered.
No one votes. One by one, the Regents just say the words. From tonight, the myth will play before every broadcast in Texas.
Metals Week.
One last order: the songs of an old country singer are to be spared by the censors.
see: a cowboy singing with a guitar

beats.text: Merciful.
No. Strategic.
